lessons.title: The Shared Responsibility Model for Data

slots.practicalActivity: For a hypothetical company storing customer data in both Azure Data Lake Storage and Amazon S3, draw the shared-responsibility line: list three things the cloud provider is responsible for versus three things the customer is responsible for, specifically for data (not infrastructure). Then sketch a one-page governance architecture diagram naming where policy enforcement, identity, and logging each live across both clouds.
slots.deliverable: A six-item shared-responsibility split for data specifically, plus a sketched cross-cloud governance architecture diagram.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch what a dedicated data-platform landing zone would need: name three policy guardrails you'd want pre-applied to every subscription or account that lands in it (e.g. mandatory encryption at rest, no public network access on storage, mandatory data-classification tags), and name whether each guardrail maps to Azure Landing Zones (management group + Azure Policy) or AWS Control Tower (guardrail + Account Factory). Then write one sentence on which guardrail must stay identical across your dev, test, and production environments.
slots.deliverable: Three named landing-zone guardrails mapped to their cloud mechanism, plus one cross-environment consistency requirement.

lessons.title: Identity and Access Management in the Cloud
Microsoft Entra ID for Data Governance

slots.practicalActivity: A hypothetical team needs read-only access to every storage account in one Azure resource group, now and in the future. Decide whether you'd assign the Reader (or Storage Blob Data Reader) role to each storage account individually or to the resource group once, and write one sentence explaining what you'd lose by choosing the per-resource approach. Then name which Entra ID directory role (not Azure RBAC) would be needed if that same team also had to manage guest user invitations.
slots.deliverable: A scope-level role-assignment decision with its reasoning, plus one named Entra ID directory role for a separate directory-level task.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a minimal AWS IAM policy (JSON) granting an analytics role s3:GetObject on a single bucket prefix only, not the whole bucket. Then compare it in one paragraph to the Azure RBAC role assignment from the previous slot: which one uses scope inheritance up a resource hierarchy, and which one relies on explicit resource ARNs in the policy document itself?
slots.deliverable: A scoped AWS IAM policy JSON document, plus a written comparison of Azure RBAC's inheritance model versus AWS IAM's explicit-ARN model.

slots.practicalActivity: Identity and access lab: for one hypothetical data platform spanning both clouds, write the real Azure 'Add role assignment' sequence (Role, Members, scope) for a team needing read access to one resource group, and the real AWS IAM policy JSON for the equivalent S3 and Glue read access. Note one access-governance pattern (just-in-time access, periodic access review, or break-glass account) you'd apply to both.
slots.deliverable: A matched pair of access grants (Azure role assignment plan and AWS IAM policy) for the same team, plus one shared access-governance pattern.

slots.practicalActivity: For a data lake split across an ADLS Gen2 container and an S3 bucket, name one governance control specific to each storage system (e.g. ADLS Gen2 hierarchical namespace ACLs versus S3 bucket policies and Block Public Access), then decide which cloud-native data catalog (Microsoft Purview or AWS Glue Data Catalog) you'd register each one into, and why having both registered in a single catalog view matters for governance.
slots.deliverable: Two storage-specific governance controls (one per cloud), plus a catalog-registration decision with its cross-cloud rationale.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the Lake Formation GRANT statement giving an AnalyticsReadOnlyRole SELECT and DESCRIBE on one table in the Glue Data Catalog using the named resource method. Then redo the same grant using Simple column-based access, excluding one sensitive column, and explain in one sentence why a plain IAM policy on the underlying S3 path couldn't achieve that column-level restriction on its own.
slots.deliverable: A full-table Lake Formation GRANT and a column-restricted version of the same grant, with the IAM-versus-Lake-Formation gap explained.

slots.practicalActivity: Storage and catalog lab: design a cross-cloud catalog strategy for a company with data in both ADLS Gen2 and S3. Name which catalog (Purview or Glue, or both federated) serves as the system of record, write one Lake Formation grant with a cell-level data filter (e.g. 'SELECT on this table, but only where region = EMEA, and never the ssn column'), and name the Azure-side equivalent fine-grained control you'd use for the same restriction.
slots.deliverable: A cross-cloud catalog strategy decision, one cell-level Lake Formation data filter grant, and its named Azure-side equivalent.

lessons.title: Encryption and Key Management in Azure and AWS

slots.practicalActivity: Decide, for a regulated dataset, whether you'd use customer-managed keys or provider-managed keys in both Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS, with one sentence of reasoning. Then assign the built-in Azure Policy 'Audit VMs that do not use managed disks' (or an equivalent storage-encryption policy) to a test resource group, and describe what you'd check on the Compliance page afterward -- and the difference between pinning that policy's version versus letting it float.
slots.deliverable: A key-management decision across both clouds, plus an assigned Azure Policy with its compliance-check plan and a pin-vs-float decision.

lessons.title: Auditing and Logging in the Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Write a service control policy (SCP) concept, in plain language, that would block every account in an AWS Organization from disabling S3 server-side encryption -- naming the effect (Deny) and the action it targets. Then name the Azure equivalent (an Azure Policy Deny effect) that would enforce the same rule, and name one centralized logging destination each cloud uses (AWS CloudTrail/Log Archive account vs. Azure Monitor/Log Analytics workspace).
slots.deliverable: A described SCP blocking an unsafe action with its Azure Policy equivalent, plus one named centralized-logging destination per cloud.

slots.practicalActivity: Security and compliance lab: for a hypothetical PCI-relevant workload running in both clouds, pick one real compliance framework (PCI DSS, HIPAA, or SOC 2) and name three specific controls it requires. Map each control to a concrete mechanism from this chapter -- an encryption setting, an Azure Policy or AWS SCP, and a logging/auditing control -- and note which cloud's mechanism you'd rely on for each.
slots.deliverable: Three compliance-framework controls mapped to concrete Azure or AWS governance mechanisms.

slots.practicalActivity: Name the single biggest multi-cloud governance challenge for a company replicating customer data between Azure and AWS (inconsistent tagging, divergent RBAC/IAM models, or duplicate catalogs), with one real example of how it shows up. Then sketch how you'd trace lineage for one piece of data that originates in an S3 bucket, gets copied into ADLS Gen2, and is finally queried from a Power BI report -- naming which tool shows which hop.
slots.deliverable: One named multi-cloud governance challenge with a concrete example, plus a sketched three-hop cross-cloud lineage trace.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the course's case study, naming the specific governance gap the fictional multi-cloud organization has at each layer (identity, storage, catalog, compliance). Complete the course's own practice lab exercise end to end, then run its review checklist against your own capstone plan (built in the final slot) and note any item it catches that you missed.
slots.deliverable: A gap analysis of the case study by governance layer, a completed practice lab, and a checklist pass noting any missed items.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a one-to-two-page multi-cloud data governance plan for a hypothetical company running data workloads in both Azure and AWS. Cover a landing-zone guardrail strategy, one identity/access control per cloud (Azure RBAC and AWS IAM or Lake Formation), a storage and catalog strategy spanning both clouds, one encryption or compliance-framework control, and how you'd trace lineage and audit access across the cloud boundary.
slots.deliverable: A one-to-two-page written multi-cloud governance plan covering landing zones, identity/access, storage/catalogs, compliance, and cross-cloud lineage and auditing.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can design governed landing zones, write real Azure RBAC role assignments and AWS IAM/Lake Formation grants down to the column and cell level, register and catalog storage across both clouds, map compliance frameworks to concrete Azure Policy and AWS Organizations controls, and trace lineage and audit access across a multi-cloud boundary -- the hands-on Azure-and-AWS governance skillset the Data Governance Engineer path assumes a student can execute end to end.
